lesson.title: The General Case: Proving d/dx of x to the n for Any Whole Number n
lesson.summary: This chapter proves the power rule for an arbitrary positive whole number exponent n using the binomial theorem, generalizing the specific case worked out earlier.
lesson.body:
The power rule chapter proved that the derivative of x^3 is 3x^2 by expanding (x+h)^3 with the binomial theorem and taking a limit. That single case is convincing, but a rule this important deserves a general argument that covers every positive whole number exponent n at once, not just n = 3. This chapter fills that gap by examining the structure of the binomial expansion for a general n.

The binomial theorem states that (x+h)^n expands as x^n + n x^(n-1) h + C(n,2) x^(n-2) h^2 + ... + n x h^(n-1) + h^n, where C(n,2) and the other coefficients in the middle are the binomial coefficients, and every term after the first involves at least one factor of h. This pattern is worth examining closely: the very first term is x^n, matching f(x) exactly, and the second term is n x^(n-1) h, carrying exactly one factor of h. Every term from the third one onward carries at least two factors of h, meaning at least h^2, h^3, and so on.

Subtracting f(x) = x^n from this expansion cancels the leading x^n term exactly, leaving f(x+h) - f(x) = n x^(n-1) h + C(n,2) x^(n-2) h^2 + ... + h^n. Every single remaining term has at least one factor of h, so dividing everything by h is valid and produces n x^(n-1) + C(n,2) x^(n-2) h + ... + h^(n-1), where now every term except the first still carries at least one leftover factor of h. Taking the limit as h approaches 0, every term with a remaining factor of h vanishes, since h itself goes to 0, and only the first term, n x^(n-1), survives untouched by the limit. This proves f'(x) = n x^(n-1) for any positive whole number n, exactly matching the power rule stated earlier.

To see this pattern concretely for a case not worked out before, take n = 4, so f(x) = x^4. Expanding, (x+h)^4 = x^4 + 4x^3 h + 6x^2 h^2 + 4x h^3 + h^4. Subtracting x^4 leaves 4x^3 h + 6x^2 h^2 + 4x h^3 + h^4, and dividing by h gives 4x^3 + 6x^2 h + 4x h^2 + h^3. As h approaches 0, every term except 4x^3 disappears, leaving f'(x) = 4x^3, which matches n x^(n-1) with n = 4 exactly. As a numeric check, at x = 3, f'(3) = 4(3)^3 = 4(27) = 108.

This general binomial argument is what secures the power rule as a fully proven fact for every positive whole number exponent, rather than something confirmed only by a handful of examples. The chapters that follow extend this same formula, n x^(n-1), to negative whole number exponents and to fractional exponents, where the binomial theorem in this exact form no longer applies directly and a different style of argument, based on algebraic manipulation of the difference quotient, is needed instead.

It is worth pausing on why only the second term of the binomial expansion, n x^(n-1) h, survives the limit while all later terms vanish. Every term from the third one onward carries at least h^2, and after dividing the whole expression by a single factor of h, those terms still retain at least one leftover factor of h each. A leftover factor of h means the term shrinks to 0 as h shrinks to 0, no matter how large its coefficient or how high the power of x sitting next to it. The second term is the unique exception: after dividing by h it has no h left at all, so it survives the limit completely unchanged, and it is precisely this surviving term that becomes the derivative formula.
